newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss government sees Holocaust fund this month.
newsitem.headline: Swiss government sees Holocaust fund this month.

text.p: The Swiss government believes a fund for Holocaust victims can be set up by the end of February using 100 million Swiss francs ($68 million) donated by banks, a government spokesman said on Wednesday.

Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti told a cabinet meeting that talks with Jewish groups and others involved in the issue had settled a number of details about the fund, vice-chancellor Achilles Casanova told reporters.

Berne said last week that it would take charge of creating the fund, including deciding on its structure with Jewish groups, gypsies and other victims of Nazi persecution, after the country's three biggest banks donated the money.

The decision, and the cabinet's willingness to consider contributing government money, persuaded the World Jewish Congress and U.S. critics to end months of pressing Switzerland to make amends for its role in World War Two.

"Many open questions about the purpose and administration of the special fund were settled, so that a solution supported by all sides can be achieved very soon," said Casanova, who acts as spokesman for the cabinet.
"There is still a realistic chance that the special fund can be set up by the end of February," Casanova told reporters in Berne.
"The cabinet stressed its desire today to carry out the creation of the special fund quickly so that those entitled to it can be helped as quickly as possible," he said.

Galvanised by international pressure, the three big banks agreed two weeks ago to put up 100 million Swiss francs as a humanitarian gesture to aid Holocaust victims and their families. Other businesses pledged to follow suit.

Berne wants the fund to assure Jewish groups and other critics that the Swiss are taking seriously allegations they cynically profited from World War Two and that banks hoarded the dormant wealth of Holocaust victims.
But a government decision on a financial commitment will have to wait for a report in the next couple of months from an international panel of historians named by Berne last December.

The panel's first task is to draw up a record of Swiss purchases of looted gold from Nazi Germany, and Switzerland's anti-Jewish wartime immigration policy that turned back 30,000 refugees -- most of them Jews -- as the Holocaust raged. (1=1.4795 Swiss Franc)
